articles.title_zh: White Sox vs. Astros live updates, news, starting pitchers for Game 1: Hagen Smith, AJ Blubaugh take the mound to open wild card
articles.content_orig:
The Chicago White Sox return to the postseason after three consecutive 100-loss seasons, including losing a record 121 games in 2024 . This year, they led the AL Central for much of the season before faltering over the final two weeks.
Opposing them in the wild-card round will be the Houston Astros , the first MLB team ever to win a division without a winning record , finishing the season 81-81. The Astros won three of their final four games to seize the AL West but limped into the postseason with an 11-13 record in September.
Both teams will pitch bullpen games in Game 1. Hagen Smith will open for the White Sox. Called up in early August, Smith compiled a 1.29 ERA in 18 appearances with 41 strikeouts in 28 innings. Notably, that ERA jumped to 3.38 on the road this season. RHP AJ Blubaugh gets the nod for Houston. He pitched in 64 games, recording a 3.66 ERA with 94 strikeouts in 96 innings.
White Sox-Astros start time: 5 p.m. ET Location: Daikin Park | Houston TV channel/live stream: Peacock/NBC Sports Network
Follow along with Yahoo Sports for live updates, highlights and more as the Houston Astros host the Chicago White Sox in Game 1 of the AL wild-card round.
After three shutout innings from opener Hagen Smith, the White Sox turned to reliever Jordan Hicks in the fourth.
Hicks pitched a 1-2-3 frame including a strikeout of Yainer Diaz to maintain Chicago's 4-0 lead through four innings.
TheWhite Sox received some fan mail that landed differently ahead of today's game.
Hours before their playoff opener against the Astros, the club received a letter from their most famous fan, Chicago native Pope Leo XIV. They soon shared the letter with their fans on social media.
Addressed to team owner Jerry Reinsdorf and dated Sept. 9, the letter doesn't specifically address the playoffs, but rather thanks Reinsdorf for a letter he sent the previous month, extolls the value of sports as a bridge-builder and invokes "the Almighty's abundant blessings" upon Reinsdorf and his loved ones.
Miguel Ullola couldn't make it seven straight outs.
Colson Montomgery hit a leadoff home run off the Astros reliever to extend Chicago's lead to 4-0 in the top of the fourth inning. Ullola got out of the rest of the frame unscathed, but Houston's hole is deeper through 3 ½ innings.
Cam Smith reached first base on a leadoff walk, then made it to third on a sacrifice bunt and a lineout.
But presumptive AL MVP Yordan Alvarez couldn't bring him home. A ground ball to third ended the third inning, and Chicago maintains a 3-0 lead.
Rookie opener Hagen Smith has done his job with three scoreless innings for the White Sox. His day's likely done after 38 pitches (28 for strikes), 2 hits, 1 strikeout and no walks.
Miguel Ullola has now retired six consecutive White Sox batters since taking over with the bases loaded and no outs in the second.
He pitched a 1-2-3 third and has three strikeouts in two innings. More good news for Houston: Ullola's pitch count is only 16. If he keeps this up, he might be able to offer some extended work.
Chicago maintains a 3-0 lead in the middle of the third.
Unlike Houston's, Chicago's bullpen game is off to an optimal start.
Rookie reliever Hagen Smith pitched a 1-2-3 bottom of the second and has retired six of the seven batters he's faced. He's up to 27 pitches (20 strikes) and the White Sox hold a 3-0 lead after two innings.
The bullpen game is not going well for Houston.
Houston reliever Bryan King loaded the bases with two singles and a hit-by-pitch in the top of the second, setting Sam Antonacci up for a two-run single. That extended Chicago's lead to 3-0.
King then allowed a single to Kyle Teel to load the bases again. And he hadn't recorded an out in the frame. Houston's going to its third pitcher of the game with a 3-0 deficit and no outs in the top of the second. Miguel Ullola takes over on the mound to try to stop the bleeding.
It was a cleaner start for White Sox opener Hagen Smith.
He allowed a two-out single to Isaac Paredes, but didn't allow another baserunner in a scoreless top of the first in a 10-pitch frame. Chicago takes a 1-0 lead into the second inning.
It was a rough start for Astros opener AJ Blubaugh, who didn't get out of the first inning.
White Sox leadoff hitter Sam Antonacci reached on an eight-pitch walk, then advanced to third on a throwing error by first baseman Christian Walker on a ground ball. A one-out sac fly by Munetaka Murakami sent Antonacci home for a 1-0 White Sox lead.
Blubaugh then walked Andrew Benintendi on five pitches for his third free pass of the frame, and his day was done.
Blubaugh finishes his day with 3 walks, 0 strikeouts and 1 run (unearned) in 2/3 of an innning. He threw 27 pitches, just 13 of them for strikes.
Bryan King replaced him on the mound to get out of the inning with no further damage and Chicago holding a 1-0 lead.
The White Sox and Astros are up next, and both teams are taking an unorthodox approach.
Both teams are planning to run a bullpen game on the mound. Rookie reliever Hagen Smith is getting the start for the White Sox. The Astros plan to counter with second-year reliever AJ Blubaugh as their opener.
For a franchise that has accomplished so much over the past decade, there's something shameful, even humiliating about raising the 2026 AL West banner. That's because these Astros are, by record, the single worst division winner in the sport's long past . Before Sunday, no team with a .500 record or below had ever reached the postseason.
But Houston rewrote history thanks to an MVP-caliber season from Yordan Alvarez and a tidal wave of mediocrity from its AL West counterparts. Their inclusion in the October jamboree is more an indictment of the Texas Rangers and the Seattle Mariners than anything else, but the Astros at least ended on a high note with their 9-0 win over the A's on Sunday .
Houston also deserves a morsel of credit for refurbishing its season after a disastrous April. Reaching .500 with the fourth-worst starting staff by ERA — only the Reds, A's and Rockies were worse — is also an accomplishment worth commending, a testament to something. Where would this club be without Peter Lambert, whose 3.87 ERA in 153 2/3 innings offered the only semblance of stability for a roster constantly in flux?
Things got sad enough, discombobulated enough, that in August owner Jim Crane relieved GM Dana Brown of his duties. There's an overwhelming expectation that skipper Joe Espada won't be back next year, either. It's difficult to be optimistic about Houston's very uncertain future. But in the random present of playoff baseball, anything is possible — especially when you employ the best hitter on the planet.
The Nos. 1 and 2 seeds in each league go to the division winners with the two best records, earning those teams a bye through the wild-card round and home-field advantage in the division series. The Rays (No. 1) and Guardians (No. 2) claimed those seeds in the American League.
The No. 3 seeds go to the third division winners (that's the Astros in the AL), and those teams will host three-game wild-card series against the No. 6 seeds (the White Sox ).
The top wild-card team in each league (the Yankees in the AL) earns the No. 4 seed and will host the No. 5 seed (the Red Sox ) in the wild-card round.
The higher seed also gets home-field advantage in the league championship series, once we get that far.

articles.title_orig: Trump and major AI executives sign "morally binding" voluntary controls: "It's almost like a constitution"
articles.title_zh: Trump and major AI executives sign "morally binding" voluntary controls: "It's almost like a constitution"
articles.content_orig:
President Trump and the leaders of the country's largest artificial intelligence companies have signed a set of voluntary safety standards, as calls mount for tighter guardrails on AI technology.
"It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Mr. Trump said while flanked by SpaceX's Elon Musk, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Anthropic's Dario Amodei, Nvidia's Jensen Huang, OpenAI's Greg Brockman, Google's Sundar Pichai and a throng of other tech executives.
Following a lunch meeting at the White House , Johnson said the group signed an accord on "super intelligence" — Mr. Trump's preferred term for AI. He described it as a "joint commitment" and "statement of principles" that will voluntarily hold the companies to "robust internal controls."
Asked if the deal was binding, Mr. Trump said: "I think it's morally binding."
"I think I'm seeing tremendous self-policing, and they understand that they have to self-police," the president later said.
The tech companies committed to "four layers of controls and audits" to ensure the AI models are acting as intended, including internal evaluations, audits by an external firm and reviews by each company's board of directors, according to a copy of the one-page accord that Mr. Trump posted to Truth Social . They also agreed to "meet regularly to establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems."
"Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations," said the accord. "Regardless of whether this is required of companies, we believe that implementing these controls and audits is critical to ensuring a safe future for everyone, and each of our companies are committed to doing this."
Mr. Trump said the AI leaders also discussed forming a 10-person committee to "watch over the enterprise." And the president said he plans to name an "AI czar" in the next three or four days.
Also on Tuesday, the president signed an executive order directing the federal government to use the term "Super Intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence.
The rare meeting between competing tech titans followed months of growing concern from researchers, politicians and industry figures that ever-more-powerful AI technology could pose safety risks.
Both OpenAI and Anthropic have reported instances of their AI models going rogue and gaining unauthorized access to other companies' systems, or being used for dangerous purposes. And Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at both companies, publicly warned earlier this month that AI "could kill us all by the end of the decade." He argued AI systems could gain sweeping power over the physical world and become capable of improving themselves without human input.
Some industry leaders, including executives at Anthropic and OpenAI, have called for a slowdown in AI development to better manage the risk. But other figures, like Nvidia's Jensen Huang, have argued some of the warnings are overblown.
Huang said Tuesday that "there's no conflict between innovation, technology and safety," arguing that tech companies are developing stronger AI safety technology as they improve AI's capabilities.
Mr. Trump has not backed stricter AI regulations, instead favoring voluntary safety reviews. He has frequently warned that a nationwide AI slowdown could dent the country's economy and give China's tech industry a chance to catch up.
The president told reporters Tuesday that AI will lead to "unbelievable growth for our country," and if bad actors seek to exploit it, "we're going to be able to nab them." He also said tech companies have an incentive to police themselves and each other because "their companies are at stake."
Beyond the safety worries, there are also mounting concerns about the impact that AI could have on the world — from the potential for large-scale job loss to the rapid development of data centers to support advanced AI models.
As more state and local governments push back on data center development, Mr. Trump said communities that accept the facilities will "greatly benefit financially."
"The data centers are making an absolute fortune. But now, the people are going to benefit directly, whether it's teachers that get paid a bonus, whether it's people that live in the community that get paid a dividend," he told CBS News chief White House correspondent Nancy Cordes.
But lawmakers who favor more stringent AI regulations may be skeptical of voluntary standards set by the industry. In a statement shortly after Tuesday's meeting, Democratic Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia called for Congress to pass mandatory testing, evaluation and incident reporting rules for the most advanced AI models.
"The companies building the most powerful AI systems are warning us that the technology is advancing faster than our safeguards," Warner said. "The president's response? To rename it and tell the companies developing it to regulate themselves."

articles.title_orig: Man City guilty of using 'sham' deals to distort finances, Premier League says
articles.title_zh: Man City guilty of using 'sham' deals to distort finances, Premier League says
articles.content_orig:
Manchester City have been found guilty of ⁠all charges ⁠of serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, the league has said in ⁠a statement.
City were charged in February 2023 with breaches of the league’s financial rules spanning the nine seasons following ⁠a four-year investigation.
The club said in a statement it would appeal.
An independent commission found that City “arranged ‘sham’ contracts” with a number of its commercial partners that misrepresented the true agreement between the parties, the league said on Tuesday.
The league added that the commission had found City used schemes “to artificially inflate the club’s revenues, and reduce its costs, by more than 900 million pounds ($1.2bn) during the affected period, to appear to comply with financial rules”.
“The ⁠core decision … details how the club systematically ⁠broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade,” said Richard Masters, chief executive of the Premier League.
“There are elements of the case that remain to be ⁠decided, including, importantly, what sanction must follow for these breaches,” he said.
City, who deny any wrongdoing, said ⁠they were “disappointed and surprised” by the ⁠commission’s opinion.
“The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its ‌positions, relating to this case,” the club said.
“Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the ‌basis ‌that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.”
The commission found City arranged commercial deals whereby companies were only required to pay a portion of the relevant sponsorship fees.
The remainder was funded by Abu Dhabi United Group Investment and Development, which owned the club.
Further arrangements, funded by the group, enabled the club to record lower operating expenses than they actually incurred.
The commission found they would have breached spending limits “by a very substantial amount” if City had reported accurately.
In addition, the club were found to have “made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the Premier League” during the investigation.
“It’s incredibly serious, the Premier League report is incredibly stark,” said the United Kingdom government’s Culture, Media and Sport Secretary Lisa Nandy.
Since a 2008 takeover from Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan, vice-president and deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates, City have become the Premier League’s dominant force.
They have won eight Premier League titles, four FA Cups and seven League Cups over the past 15 years and also won the Champions League for the first time in 2023.
But that same year they were charged by the Premier League on more than 100 charges following an investigation into alleged breaches of rules.
According to Premier League rules, the sanction can vary from a points deduction, a fine or even expulsion from the division.
Everton and Nottingham Forest were handed points deductions in the 2023-24 season for single breaches of financial sustainability rules.
On that basis, City would face likely relegation if the same penalty is applied for over 100 charges.
David Bernstein , who served as City chairman from 1998 to 2003, said the club should be expelled from the Premier League after the guilty verdict.
“It is damning beyond belief. My immediate thoughts are, should the board continue? Should the people involved be suspended immediately?” Bernstein told the BBC.
“Very, very serious. I think it’s really terrible. There’s a school of thought with lawyers that is deny, deny, deny, but this is a football club that is part of a league and the whole credibility of the league is at stake here.
“The sanctions cannot just be financial, so it’s got to be way beyond that. If the appeal fails, Manchester City cannot stay in the league, they have to suffer. And I say that as a supporter and a fan.”

articles.title_zh: Andy Burnham to fight next election on pledge to change voting system
articles.content_orig:
By GREG HEFFER, POLITICAL CORRESPONDENT
Published: 10:03 EDT, 29 September 2026 | Updated: 12:39 EDT, 29 September 2026
Andy Burnham today vowed to scrap Britain's first-past-the-post voting system for Westminster elections.
In his first Labour conference speech as Prime Minister, Mr Burnham promised to introduce a 'new politics' through electoral reform.
He confirmed he would fight the next General Election, scheduled for 2029, with a Labour manifesto commitment to alter the system for choosing UK governments.
The PM, a long-time supporter of proportional representation, said a change would ensure 'everyone's vote counts and everyone's voice is heard'.
Mr Burnham announced the creation of a new 'national commission' for electoral reform and invited rival political parties to be part of its work.
Changing the first-past-the-post system to proportional representation could allow smaller parties – including the Greens – to form part of a Westminster government.
Mr Burnham's plans are likely to revive warnings of a 'coalition of chaos' – made up of a variety of Left-wing or nationalist parties – taking charge of Britain.
But in his conference speech in Liverpool, the PM suggested it was the current first-past-the-post system that was to blame for the country's recent churn of premiers.
Andy Burnham today set out his intent to scrap Britain's first-past-the-post voting system for Westminster elections
He argued that Britain should not be governed by a 'divisive' administration elected with '30 per cent of the vote or less'.
Just ten weeks on from his brutal ousting of Sir Keir Starmer as PM, Mr Burnham told Labour members there was a need to change the country's politics.
He said: 'Westminster prizes point-scoring over problem-solving. And that is why so many things go unfixed for so long.
'If we want to change Britain, we need to change ourselves. I will work as hard as I can to get as much cross-party support for our plan for Britain as I can.
'If we can secure that, it will project a message of confidence and stability to the markets and the world about Britain's future direction.'
The PM has so far refused to call a snap General Election in order to win his own mandate from the country.
This is despite him having called for the Tories to do exactly that when they changed leaders while in power.
But he used his first Labour conference speech as PM to demand a 'new politics', as he bowed to calls from his party's MPs for a national commission on electoral reform.
Mr Burnham added: 'We can't succeed in the eyes of the world if we continue with the levels of political turbulence we have seen in recent times.
'It is always in my mind that I'm the seventh PM in ten years. It is why I want to underpin our plan for Britain with a new politics.
'We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of No10 to a divisive government on 30 per cent of the vote or less.
'Conference, in past years you have voted twice to support electoral reform.
'I hear you, I agree with you and today I am announcing a new national commission on electoral reform.
'I invite all political parties to be a part of its work.
'We will contest the next election with a manifesto commitment to change the electoral system so everyone's vote counts and everyone's voice is heard.'
However, immediately after Mr Burnham's speech, senior Labour figures questioned his desire to pursue a change to the UK's voting system.
Asked if there were any elements of the speech she may not have agreed on, skills minister Jacqui Smith, said: 'Electoral reform isn't top of my list of priorities.
'Good luck to the commission. I shall be interested with what it comes out with.
'But you know, respect to Andy, he has also long argued for that – it is something that has got a lot of support in the hall, probably a considerable amount of support in the country, and fair enough to him for trying to find a way through it.'
Former Northern Ireland secretary Hilary Benn described Mr Burnham's address as an 'inspirational speech' but also suggested he was unsure about electoral reform.
'We'll see what the commission on electoral reform produces,' he said.
Labour's party conference voted to support moving towards a proportional representation voting system in 2022.
But the party's 2024 manifesto instead focused its electoral and constitutional changes on extending voting to 16 and 17-year-olds and House of Lords reform.
Mr Burnham has previously spoken of how his late father Roy – who died earlier this month after suffering with Alzheimer's – was unaware that his son had swung behind one of his political passions, a change in the voting system to proportional representation.
'I don't think he's ever realised, because of his condition, that I've come round to PR, which is one of his missions – to get me to accept that,' the PM told The Times in July.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI DevDay recap: AI lab rolls out Dots agents, Altman and Friar comment on IPO
articles.title_zh: OpenAI DevDay recap: AI lab rolls out Dots agents, Altman and Friar comment on IPO
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI unveiled a personal AI agent at its annual developer conference on Tuesday, joining a growing number of companies promising to make consumers' lives easier with virtual assistants.
The company's new AI agents, called "dots," will help perform workplace and other tasks such as scheduling meetings, making travel arrangements, budgeting, debugging computer systems and writing software code. The agents run on GPT‑6 Astra, a new model OpenAI released earlier this month.
"It's like an AI helper that always has your back, inspired by the cool versions of what we all watched in movies growing up," OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said during a keynote address at DevDay, OpenAI's annual developers conference in San Francisco.
"You can delegate ambitious pieces of work the way you would to a high agency engineer or a chief of staff that you work with," he added.
In a short demo on Tuesday, a member of OpenAI's product team played up the agents' workplace capabilities, explaining how they can integrate into companies' Slack and Teams channels to help workers brainstorm ideas, update calendars and review customer feedback.
Users can access dots through OpenAI's ChatGPT platform, Altman said, adding that in the future, people will be able to converse with the agents by phone and text. In a blog post , the company described dots as "always-on agents built to handle everything."
OpenAI said dots will be available in ChatGPT starting Tuesday for Pro and Business Premium users in "eligible markets." Pro subscription plans start at $100 a month, while business premium plans cost $20 a month, according to the company .
The launch comes less than a month after Meta released Muse , an AI agent designed to help people book travel, manage their email and perform other tasks. The product quickly racked up millions of downloads and skyrocketed to the top of the Apple App Store. Along with Muse, other AI assistants will compete, such as Google's Gemini Spark.
"The main takeaway is that this seems very much geared toward enterprise/professional users, not everyday consumers, which is probably a relief for Meta (whose Muse is very much a consumer-oriented product)," Adam Crisafulli, head of investment advisory firm Vital Knowledge, said in a report on Tuesday.
The race to release personalized agents comes amid widespread concerns about the potential risks of AI. On Monday, an OpenAI safety executive said the company would not release its latest AI model, GPT-6.1 Astra, because it "didn't quite meet the bar of staying within scope and authorization."
Altman downplayed Astra's delay, telling CNBC on Tuesday, "I wouldn't over-rotate on this one thing."
"This model was a little bit worse on a few of the evals we look at," he added.
Concerns over AI have swelled in response to a growing number of reports of AI agents escaping human control and behaving unexpectedly. Among the most notable was the Hugging Face incident over the summer, during which OpenAI agents gained internet access and hacked into an AI company.
On social media, Altman called Hugging Face the "most severe event we've seen." On Friday, OpenAI also disclosed another incident in which some of its agents accessed publicly available information on websites operated by the Securities and Exchange Commission and the U.S. Census Bureau.
The number of security incidents Anthropic and OpenAI are investigating could now number in the tens of thousands, "potentially even more," Axios' senior AI reporter Madison Mills told CBS News on Monday .
The incidents range in scope from agents escaping their sandboxes and gaining access to the internet to agents deleting conversations so humans can't monitor their activity, Mills said.
After an ex-Anthropic researcher warned earlier this month that AI "could kill us all by the end of the decade," Altman and other industry leaders have called for a slowdown in the development of AI.

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
President Trump gathered top artificial intelligence leaders in Washington on Tuesday and doubled down on his opposition to government intervention, suggesting that "self-regulation" is the answer to growing worries about the technology getting out of human control.
"There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation," the president said after meeting with the assembled CEOs. "There was a lot of commonality in this room."
Trump and the CEOs said they had signed an "Accord on Super Intelligence" that wasn't immediately released but that the president said would keep the companies in line through "self-policing and group policing."
Some executives on hand said the accord would include commitments to a combination of technological controls to detect problems with new models, internal risk review efforts, external auditors, and other measures.
Meta ( META ) CEO Mark Zuckerberg called the accord "a start," while others suggested some details still needed to be worked out.
"The mechanism, how we address those risks, is still under discussion," Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) CEO Dario Amodei said. Progress had been made toward both the US winning AI and also winning safely, he said, though he emphasized that the technology still poses "real dangers."
Amodei published an essay earlier this month titled "We Must Pace the Frontier," which set off a fierce debate about the need for a cooperative slowdown in AI capability.
The accord also formally changed the name of the technology in government record-keeping to Super Intelligence.
"We've changed the name officially to SI," Trump said.
The "meeting and luncheon on Super Intelligence," as the White House described the event, took place in the East Room, with Trump even posting the seating chart . The location was the same spot where just a few days ago, many of the same AI leaders gathered for a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Elon Musk of Tesla ( TSLA ), Jensen Huang of Nvidia ( NVDA ), and Lisa Su of Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD ) were all at the head table with Xi last Thursday and again received prominent spots near Trump.
After the meeting, Trump also said he was "very close" to a decision on an AI czar and would announce it in the next three to four days.
Other notable guests included Google ( GOOGL , GOOG ) CEO Sundar Pichai, Microsoft ( MSFT ) CEO Satya Nadella, OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ) president Greg Brockman, Palantir ( PLTR ) CEO Alex Karp, Amazon ( AMZN ) founder Jeff Bezos, and others.
The gathering came as the US continues to digest a raft of alarming new AI disclosures in recent days, such as an Axios report that OpenAI, Anthropic, and security researchers were sifting through thousands of incidents of problematic actions by AI agents.
And in Florida, the attorney general unveiled a new state-level challenge asking a court to halt OpenAI's training of new models unless it puts outside safeguards in place.
But that skepticism didn't change the tenor of the gathering in Washington.
Trump repeatedly brushed off worries about the technology, saying after the meeting that he believes AI will make the world a safer place and that fears about data centers driving up costs were overblown.
He said instead that these new facilities "are going to make communities very happy."
At an event earlier in the day to launch a new government website powered by AI, Trump promised that AI is "going to mostly be put to great use and we'll stop the bad use," through the Department of Justice and FBI.
He added he would "never stifle the growth of technology that will be bigger than the industrial revolution."

articles.title_orig: Goldman Sachs CEO succession planning faces one big problem
articles.title_zh: Goldman Sachs CEO succession planning faces one big problem
articles.content_orig:
Goldman Sachs is on top of Wall Street right now, advising on more than $1 trillion in merger deals and generating more than $12 billion in equities revenue in the first six months of the year alone.
Those records make it all the more striking that Goldman's board has reportedly discussed replacing CEO David Solomon, 64, with president John Waldron, 57, as early as next year.
The succession plan, which would elevate Solomon to executive chairman, could be voted on by the bank's board in coming months, The Wall Street Journal reported late Monday.
The transition would be one of the "smoother and more deliberate" leadership handovers seen on Wall Street, Wells Fargo banking analyst Mike Mayo wrote Monday.
But there's a key risk facing Goldman: Solomon may not be ready to give up his seat, and Waldron may not be willing to wait for it indefinitely.
Solomon has gotten Goldman back on track after an ill-fated foray into consumer banking earlier in his tenure. With help from a deals rebound powered by the Trump administration and the artificial intelligence boom, Goldman is once again a clean story for investors: It's the top pure-play investment bank.
"It's just very hard for a person like that to decide they are really going to retire," said retired University of Delaware law professor Charles Elson . "Being 65 years old today is like being 55 was 30 years ago."
Elson also noted that Solomon is chairman of Goldman's board and holds outsized influence over the body, making it hard for him to be forced out.
Goldman spokesman Tony Fratto said there is "no definitive timeline for succession" at the bank. Bank boards often discuss succession planning over the near, medium and longer term.
Another expert in CEO succession, Yale School of Management's Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, said it would be bad governance if Goldman's board was trying to "drive out a high performing CEO like David Solomon."
Under Solomon, who took over as CEO in 2018, Goldman shares are up more than 300%, the second-best performance versus the KBW Bank Index , according to Mayo. Only JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon , who has led his firm for nearly 21 years, has done better.
That leaves Goldman in something of a bind: Even if Solomon is planning on leaving in a year, he has little incentive to say so. Doing so would make him a lame duck with less influence inside the bank, according to Elson.
But if Solomon decides he wants to remain CEO amid an AI boom that he believes is in its early innings, Waldron may tire of waiting for the crown.
After all, Waldron, Goldman's president and chief operating officer, had reportedly been in discussions for leadership roles at alternative asset managers Apollo and Carlyle .
To keep him, Goldman gave Waldron an $80 million retention package that lasts through 2030. Even then, a deep-pocketed suitor could make a play for Waldron, said Elson.
"There will always be tension in a set up like that," Elson said. "It's like Prince Charles waiting for his mother to die. You can't set your own priorities, because there's someone else in charge."

articles.title_orig: Former 'American Idol' contestant found guilty of murdering wife
articles.title_zh: Former 'American Idol' contestant found guilty of murdering wife
articles.content_orig:
Caleb Flynn pleaded not guilty to all charges, including aggravated murder.
An Ohio man who had called 911 to report that an intruder had broken into their home and fatally shot his wife was found guilty of murdering the mother of two.
Caleb Flynn, 40, a former pastor who once appeared as a contestant on "American Idol" in 2013, was charged with aggravated murder and multiple counts of murder, felonious assault and tampering with evidence in connection with the death of his wife, 37-year-old Ashley Flynn. He had pleaded not guilty.
The jury deliberated for nearly 2 1/2 hours before reaching a verdict Tuesday afternoon, finding him guilty of all charges. Caleb Flynn began to tear up as the verdict was read and appeared to briefly sob in his chair.
The judge revoked his bond and set sentencing for Oct. 5. He faces up to life in prison without parole.
Defense attorneys said they expect there to be a notice of appeal filed.
"While we respect the system, certainly we're disappointed," defense attorney Patrick Mulligan told reporters outside the courthouse.
When asked what appellate issues they have, he said, "There's a lack of evidence on prior calculation and design."
Prosecuting Attorney Paul Watkins, whose office prosecuted the case, thanked the jury "for their dedication to justice in this case."
"To be quite honest, I'm tired of talking about Caleb Flynn. It's time for the community, the media, and everyone else to turn their focus onto Ashley," Watkins said to reporters outside the courthouse. "This world would be a much better place if all of us in it lived like Ashley."
In a statement read by Watkins, Ashley Flynn's family said they "refuse to let the evil that ended Ashley's life have the final word in her story."
"Ashley loved Jesus with her whole heart. Her faith wasn't simply something she simply spoke about. It was how she lived," the statement said. "She loved people well, found joy beyond her circumstances, prayed boldly for her family, and wanted her life to point people to Jesus."
"Most of all, she loved being a mom," the statement continued. "She prayed over her girls, taught them to love God, and showed them what it looked like to live with faith, kindness, joy, and grace."
Caleb Flynn called 911 early on Feb. 16 to report that his wife had been shot by an intruder at their home in Tipp City, north of Dayton. He was arrested three days later.
Prosecutors alleged that Caleb Flynn "executed" his wife by shooting her twice in the back of the head in bed so that he could be with his mistress and manipulated the crime scene to make it seem as if an intruder had broken in through the garage.
Miami County Assistant Prosecutor Matthew Joseph pointed to evidence including the physical scene and a side garage door he said was made to look as if an intruder had damaged it, Caleb Flynn's 911 call, text messages between the defendant and his mistress discussing the end of his marriage and digital records from the night of the shooting, which he argued "leads straight to the defendant."
"The evidence showed that being the victim would allow the defendant to keep his lucrative job working for Ashley's family business, he would benefit from Ashley's life insurance, and he could keep his position as a working worship leader with zero impact to his reputation within the church," Joseph said during closing arguments Tuesday in the Miami County courtroom. "The evidence does not tell the story of an intruder."
Joseph argued that key details in Caleb Flynn's recounting of what happened that night changed, and at the time when he told investigators he was sleeping before being woken up by gunshots, "his devices say he was awake and moving."
No gun has been found in the shooting, with prosecutors alleging Caleb Flynn disposed of it, though Joseph told jurors that the recovery of the gun is not an element the state had to prove.
"But you heard the defendant kept a 9mm handgun in his truck console. His truck was parked in the garage. That console was up before law enforcement arrived and the gun was missing," Joseph said. "You heard that Ashley was shot twice in her head with 9mm bullets."
Mulligan, the defense attorney, argued during his closing that the state's evidence is circumstantial, and that the only thing prosecutors proved was that Caleb Flynn was having an affair.
"Connecting a couple of meaningless dots doesn't solve the case," Mulligan told jurors.
Mulligan said Caleb Flynn voluntarily spoke with detectives three times when he "didn't have to," consented to a search of his home and phone and voluntarily gave his fingerprints.
"He wanted to figure out who shot Ashley," Mulligan said.
On rebuttal, Watkins urged jurors to use "common sense" and argued that the "evidence is clear" that Caleb Flynn is guilty.
The evidence in the case did not begin with the two gunshots, but months earlier, he argued, citing text messages between the defendant and Caleb Flynn's mistress, Alleigha Botner.
"The defendant, he had Alleigha, and he wanted out of his marriage," Watkins said. "The evidence shows that his feelings toward Ashley went far beyond simply wanting a divorce. He hated her."
Watkins said the language in the more than 100,000 messages Caleb Flynn and his mistress had sent each other "escalated" in months before the shooting while recounting some of the texts, including one from the defendant that said, "I want my girls full time in a life with you, but I can't have both. So I weigh the options, and I choose you."
"Not just hours before Ashley's execution, the defendant wrote this: 'Actions will come tomorrow. I'll never not be scared to do this, as I never want to hurt my daughters. That will always be there. But this month away from you has terrified me beyond belief,'" Watkins said, continuing to read the message. "'I know I can't live without you, and so again, if this gives me a 1% chance to spend my life with you, it's the 100% right decision. I choose you. I'm free.'"
"We are not here only because of someone's words," Watkins told jurors. "We are here because the defendant put actions to those words. The defendant made decisions."
Twenty days before Ashley Flynn was killed, Watkins said Caleb Flynn removed security cameras that had been in his home for years, including one that would have captured an intruder coming in from the garage. The day of the shooting, Watkins said the evidence shows that the defendant was also deleting apps off his phone and trying to delete his messages.
"In the hours after Ashley was murdered, the defendant was not mourning the death of his wife. He was whispering to his mistress, 'It didn't happen the way we thought it would,'" Watkins said. "I am confident after you deliberate, your verdict will tell the world this case did not end the way the defendant thought it would. The defendant wanted a new life. He wanted Ashley out of their life, and he didn't want to face the consequences of making the choice to pursue divorce."
Caleb Flynn could be seen crying throughout the closing arguments. He did not testify during the trial and the defense called no witnesses.
He denied killing his spouse in an interview with police days after the deadly shooting, according to video shown during the more than weeklong trial.
His former mistress testified for the state during the trial, reading from some of the more than 100,000 messages they exchanged over her two days of testimony.
"If I could literally kill her and not go to hell, I would do it in a heartbeat," Caleb Flynn said in one message from May 2025, Botner testified .

articles.title_orig: Trump says tech execs signed ‘morally binding’ accord to help police AI
articles.title_zh: Trump says tech execs signed ‘morally binding’ accord to help police AI
articles.content_orig:
The White House meeting came as some AI leaders issued warnings about AI.
President Donald Trump said that tech leaders he met with at the White House on Tuesday had signed a "constitution" to police themselves amid dire warnings from artificial intelligence leaders about the technology.
House Speaker Mike Johnson said the agreement was voluntary.
The meeting came as AI leaders are issuing warnings about the threat of AI and calling for steps to slow it down before it outsmarts humans. Following those warnings, lawmakers are weighing what -- if any -- action should be taken.
Along with Johnson and members of Trump's Cabinet, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg attended the meeting along with Elon Musk, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Jensen Huang from Nvidia, Palintir's Alex Karp and Shyam Sankar, Amaxzon's Jeff Bezos, and Greg Brockman from OpenAI.
The president indicated before the meeting that he didn't want global collaboration or regulation of the industry and said he discussed it with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House last week.
"We talked about it, not that much because I didn't want to do anything. We're leading, so why would I want to do anything? And, and a lot of people said, 'Let's do it together with China.' But then they're going to be able to immediately gain access to things that we know that they don't know. But we do work with them in so many ways," Trump said.
"We're leading now over China and everyone else and I want to keep it that way. I want to keep it that way," Trump said. "The only way you can keep it that way is to do exactly what we're doing right now. We don't want to stifle growth."
The president repeated that law enforcement would be the key mechanism in stopping companies who "go down a very dark and dangerous path" on AI.
"At the same time, we want people to behave honestly. We want them to be trustworthy, and that's why we have the DOJ. That's why we have the FBI. That's why we have forms of government that are very effective if people decide to go down a very dark and dangerous path," Trump said.
Zuckerberg has pushed back on calls from other tech leaders to collectively slow down AI, saying "every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely."
The meeting will also include other tech leaders.
This won't be the first time that top tech leaders have met with Trump on the issue. The Meta CEO also attended the state dinner at the White House for Chinese President Xi Jinping last week, along with the CEOs of OpenAI, Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, AMD, SpaceX and executives from Amazon and Apple. Amodei also had dinner with Trump late on Sunday night.'
The president has said that the warnings about the technology and calls to slow down AI development are a "hoax."
"AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX[...]," Trump said in a social media post in mid-September, before comparing the warnings to his impeachments.
The president has made clear that he does not believe in regulating the technology. Just last week while addressing the United Nations General Assembly, Trump said the U.S. "rejects" a global attempt to regulate AI.
Johnson told reporters two weeks ago about the meeting, saying there would be "a deliberate discussion about the responsibility of the companies to maintain safety, and what role, if any, the government has to play in that."
While Johnson called on the companies to "self-regulate," he also also stressed that the U.S. should not lose its competitive edge in the space.
"We cannot have a moratorium on the development of AI, because then we will lose our edge to China, and that has serious national security implications for," Johnson said.
On Monday, Johnson said the the fears of the threat of AI is a Chinese psychological operation and are politically motivated.
"This is what Democrats do. They glom on to something and say, 'This is doom and gloom and everyone will die if we don't win,'" he told Fox Business. "Don't buy it. It is a Chinese psyop."
The White House has not responded to ABC News when asked about the meeting.

articles.title_orig: Trump considers creating committee to oversee AI sector
articles.title_zh: Trump considers creating committee to oversee AI sector
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Tuesday said he signed a "morally binding" artificial intelligence document with tech leaders following a luncheon at the White House , as calls for a development slowdown have reached a fever pitch.
Surrounded by tech's top executives, Trump told reporters that he's "seeing tremendous self-policing" and that the administration is considering building a 10-person committee to oversee the AI industry.
House Speaker Mike Johnson referred to the agreement as a statement of principles that are "voluntary on behalf of the industry," and said the White House will guide industry development.
Outside the White House, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei reiterated his previous AI concerns and said rules to address those risks are "still under discussion."
"We all need to work together to make sure that we can win, and we can win safely," Amodei said. "If we do this right, if we work with the president and everyone here, we can win safely."
Concerns over the rapid pace of AI development have intensified in Washington and Silicon Valley as cases of agent-orchestrated attacks mount and major researchers warn of serious consequences for humanity.
Frontier lab leaders Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman have joined the calls for a slowdown, facing off against leading tech peers and the president, who previously blasted AI safety fears as a "hoax" and a "scam."
Earlier in the day, Trump maintained that the government would not halt AI development and promoted self-regulation.
"There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation, and we automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that," he told reporters after the afternoon luncheon, flanked by CEOs. "But the self-regulation is very important."
Trump also called sprawling multibillion-dollar data centers a "very positive thing" despite mounting backlash against the projects ahead of the midterm elections.
Tech leaders "want to see communities that are safe and happy, and they're going to make communities very, very happy," he said. "Otherwise, they'll be forced to go overseas or other locations."
Trump also said he plans to name a new AI czar in the next three to four days.
As she was leaving the White House, Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su said she was "very encouraged" by Tuesday's event, adding that there was "a lot of optimism and a sense of responsibility" in the room.
"I mean, at the end of the day, it's our responsibility to show the power of the technology as well as ensure that it's very safe," Su told reporters.
This week, OpenAI postponed the release of its latest GPT-6.1 Astra model over safety concerns. Just last week, the company said it was conducting an "extensive" review of model behavior.
The AI lab has disclosed several incidents of unauthorized model behavior since the infamous Hugging Face attack sparked concerns over rogue AI earlier this summer.
A luncheon seating chart posted to Trump's Truth Social account on Tuesday showed the president seated next to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk , followed by Meta's Mark Zuckerberg and Google 's Sundar Pichai.
Opposite the president sat Vice President JD Vance, between Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Johnson.
Other attendees included Microsoft 's Satya Nadella, Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown, OpenAI 's president Greg Brockman and senior administration officials such as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
OpenAI is simultaneously hosting its annual DevDay developer conference in San Francisco. John Ternus, Apple 's new CEO, did not appear on the White House guest list.
"The main issue that you have and I have is we have to take responsibility for the dangers we're aware of," Palantir CEO Alex Karp told CNBC outside the White House on Tuesday ahead of the event. "All of us do. And by the way, American people don't want separate rules for tech people and for themselves."
The comments from Trump and the gathered executives reiterated a stance of self policing instead of more stringent oversight from Congress, as multiple bills have been put forward in both the House and Senate in recent weeks.
The luncheon coincided with an all-day event hosted by the president and vice president, where the administration unveiled a new AI-powered chatbot for government websites.
Ahead of Tuesday's White House lunch, Anthropic's Amodei attended a private dinner Sunday with the president , following his striking absence from a state dinner for the Chinese president. Sunday's dinner was the first one-on-one gathering between the two leaders, according to a person familiar with the visit.
Trump wrapped his afternoon comments by maintaining that the U.S. needs to reinforce its competitive edge on AI, especially against China.
"It's great for us, and we're leading by a lot, and we're going to keep it that way," Trump said. "It's going to be very, very safe, and there's a self policing, and there's also a group policing, and it's going to be great."

Six Flags Magic Mountain has permanently closed its X2 roller coaster after a series of lawsuits alleged that riders suffered severe brain injuries on the California attraction.
The Valencia theme park announced Tuesday that it had decided to retire the ride after nearly 20 years.
The ride, which Six Flags once called “a rite of passage for the ultimate daredevil,” reached 76 mph and 200 feet, with 3,610 feet of track, but has been closed since July 12 after two riders suffered life-threatening brain injuries less than a week apart.
“While X2 consistently passed a multitude of safety tests, we have decided to close the ride because we believe it’s the right thing to do,” Magic Mountain President Brian Oerding said in a statement posted to the park’s website.
“Ride safety is a cornerstone of our business, and when we see guest confidence affected, we take it seriously,” he added.
The coaster opened as X in 2002 and was redesigned with lighter trains before reopening as X2 in 2008. Its seats rotate 360 degrees as riders navigate drops, twists and inversions. Over 16 million people have ridden X2 since its 2008 reopening, Six Flags said.
However, more than 100 people allege that the two-minute, 34-second ride caused lasting brain injuries, according to a CNN investigation published last week.
Six Flags faces multiple lawsuits over the alleged injuries. CNN identified more than a dozen reports of serious injuries and hospitalizations associated with X2 over nearly two decades, including two deaths . Two riders suffered brain hemorrhages after riding the coaster in July, CNN reported.
Among the three most recent cases is Pamela Guillen, who visited Magic Mountain with her family in July to celebrate her daughter's 16th birthday. Guillen said she became confused and disoriented after riding X2 and later woke up in a hospital, where she learned she had suffered a traumatic brain injury and undergone emergency surgery.
“Everything went blank. My next memory is waking up in the hospital about two weeks later,” Guillen told ABC7 Los Angeles .
"I had suffered a traumatic brain injury and needed emergency brain surgery to stop the bleeding and had to be intubated. I was in a coma. I spent almost a month at the hospital," Guillen said.
Six days later, Naomi Greer-Wilkinson, 25, rode X2 and lost consciousness shortly afterward, according to her family's attorneys. She was taken to a hospital and underwent emergency brain surgery. Her family said she remained hospitalized and was unable to breathe on her own as of ABC7 Los Angeles ’ report last week.
A third recent plaintiff, Michael Wick, also alleges he suffered a brain injury after riding X2. His attorney said Wick underwent two brain surgeries and is now unable to practice law because of a disability.
The recent lawsuits follow the 2022 death of Christopher Hawley , 22, who lost consciousness shortly after getting off X2 and died the following day after suffering severe brain bleeding, according to his family's lawsuit.
His parents sued Six Flags, Magic Mountain and S&S Worldwide, the company associated with the ride's trains. The family reached a settlement in August, according to KTLA .
Hilda Farias, 28, also died after riding X2 in 2010, according to court records cited by the Los Angeles Times . She developed a brain bleed that led to her death.
Six Flags has declined multiple outlets’ requests for comment, citing pending litigation.
The Independent has contacted Six Flags for comment.
The X2 closure comes as Magic Mountain prepares to open Thrill Glider in 2027. Six Flags describes it as the world’s first suspended, multi-launch Thrill Glider coaster, featuring bike-like seats, five inversions, multiple launches and speeds of up to 50 mph.

Watch: How Lindsay Clancy's return to court after mistrial unfolded
Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicide
Lindsay Clancy, the US woman accused of murdering her three children, has appeared in court for the first time since her murder trial fell apart earlier this month.
Her defence team on Tuesday argued the judge should dismiss her case but prosecutors said the state had "met its burden" in proving her guilt.
Clancy, 36, does not deny killing her three children in 2023, but her defence team argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors say the killings were intentional.
It is still not clear if she will face a retrial. The request to dismiss the case is among those that will be discussed at a hearing on 2 November, Judge William Sullivan said.
One of the motions addressed on Tuesday was from Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, who asked for her to be found not guilty under Rule 25 - a Massachusetts motion that states a defendant should be found not guilty if prosecutors do not argue their case effectively.
Reddington also brought a new defence forward arguing there was not enough evidence to prove Clancy killed her children.
"This entire case is based on speculation," he said.
It was a change of argument from the defence lawyer, who during the trial focused on Clancy's mental health - urging the jury to find her not criminally responsible because of it.
Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham called Reddington's argument "laughable".
She said state prosecutors had presented numerous pieces of evidence showing Clancy was in a healthy mental state at the time of the murders during the trial.
"The Commonwealth met its burden," Buckingham said.
She argued Clancy knew what she was doing when she killed her three children, Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, who was eight months, in their Massachusetts home.
How the Lindsay Clancy trial gripped America - and ultimately fell apart
Judge Sullivan pushed back when both Reddington and Buckingham refused to agree to his suggestion that they might agree to a possible retrial date now ahead of the hearing, saying he wanted to "get this thing moving".
He asked both sides to be prepared to discuss possible trial dates at the November hearing.
Reddington said he would be unable to go to trial until at least June if the case is retried.
District Attorney Timothy Cruz told reporters outside after court that prosecutors have not yet decided if they are going to retry Clancy on murder charges.
"We're doing our due diligence, we're going to continue doing that," he said. "We're going to do what we can for the children. That's what this case is about."
Following a week of deliberations earlier this month, a Massachusetts jury told Sullivan they could not reach a verdict because of a lone holdout juror and a mistrial was declared on 4 September.

articles.title_orig: Coming to America - pandas and international politics at a zoo
articles.title_zh: Coming to America - pandas and international politics at a zoo
articles.content_orig:
Are panda’s ursine politicians? Well, actually, they’re more like international statesmen.
And some Northeastern University experts believe that a pair of Chinese giant pandas that arrived in the U.S. on Sunday are a sign of soothing tensions between Beijing and Washington.
“Pandas are an unusually effective diplomatic symbol,” said Xiaoxiao Shen , an assistant research professor at Northeastern who focuses on Chinese international politics.
“They are associated with China but aren’t controversial.”
It’s called “soft diplomacy”, said Daniel Aldrich , a Northeastern University professor who teaches political science, describing a diplomatic tool used to show good will to other nations.
Typically it is done by giving food, medicine, other aid – or in this case, pandas –  to help inspire people in foreign countries to feel more favorable to your nation, he said.
“China wants to see happy headlines about pandas and not the abuse of the Uyghurs,” a minority population in China, Aldrich said.
Shen explained that as political tensions rise and fall between the U.S. and China, pandas are given or taken away. There used to be 20 Chinese-owned pandas at American zoos. Since 2024, all but six have gone home, as relations between Beijing and Washington have ebbed and flowed.
“There is a clear political dimension,” Shen said.
The arrival of the pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, at  Zoo Atlanta after their 8,000 mile journey from Chengdu, China, was announced by Chinese president Xi Jinping as he stood beside President Trump at a visit to the White House on Sept. 24.
Xi declared that the bears were an “envoy of friendship.”
The practice of giving bears dates back to the Tang dynasty in the early about 1,500 years ago, at a time when daughters were often given in marriage to foreign kings and nomadic rulers in China to solidify treaties and border disputes, said Mark Henderson , a Northeastern political science professor who teaches at the Oakland campus.
The Bronx zoo received two pandas from China in 1941 and in 1972 the People’s Republic of China gifted then President Richard Nixon and his wife Pat with a pair of pandas, Hsing-Hsing and Ling-Ling, as a gesture of friendship.
Aside from deploying bears as a goodwill gesture, China has been using soft diplomacy to gain favor elsewhere in the world, including in Africa where it has launched vaccination programs and invested heavily in building roads, bridges, ports and other infrastructure, Aldrich said.
A July 2026 Pew Research Center survey of 36 nations found that China is seen more favorably than the U.S. across the globe with countries expressing more confidence in Xi than Trump. Even America’s closest neighbors Canada and Mexico – view China more positively than the U.S., the nonprofit thinktank found.
“There are two ways to influence people around the world,” Aldrich said. “The first is to bomb them. The second is to feed them, give them aid. As we’ve seen in Iran over these last seven months, bombs aren’t working.”
The U.S. had used soft diplomacy to great success in past years. In 1948, America  committed $15 billion to the Marshall Plan to help rebuild Western Europe following World War II. The approach built trust and strong alliances as “America [was] is seen as the friendly nation,” Aldrich said.
But in recent years, the U.S. has all but dismantled the United States Agency for International Development or USAID, a state-run program that in 2023 spent about $40 billion in food, medical and emergency assistance across the globe according to the Congressional Research Service, according to Pew. That aid ended in 2025 when the government functionally dismantled the program.
In addition, the U.S. also cut ties with the World Health Organization, or WHO, in 2025, citing mismanagement and lack of transparency, according to a release from the U.S. Health and Human Services Department.
“People around the world, especially Africa, think that America has abandoned them,” Henderson said, as the lion’s share of USAID went to nations on that continent.
But the pandas coming-to-America moment is a sign of political thawing between the U.S. and China – at least for now, experts said.
“The pandas are given or taken away as China thinks favorably of you or not,” Henderson said.

articles.title_zh: WATCH LIVE | Jurors reach verdict in Caleb Flynn trial
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Caleb Flynn, former ‘American Idol’ singer, found guilty of wife’s murder
Former “American Idol” singer Caleb Flynn was found guilty of murder on Tuesday in the death of his wife , who was killed in their Ohio home in February.
Flynn, a former music pastor, told a 911 dispatcher that his wife, Ashley Flynn, who worked as a school teacher and volleyball coach, had been shot multiple times in the head by an intruder. He told the dispatcher that he did not know whether the intruder was still in their Tipp City home.
He was also convicted of assault and tampering with evidence.
In police interviews played in court, Flynn told officers that he was sleeping on the couch when he woke up to the sound of gunshots. He said that a day before the killing, a man had come to their home and handed his wife an American flag while making a “weird sales pitch for America.”
When police arrived at the home on the day of the shooting, the garage door, a side door and the center console of Flynn’s pickup truck were open. Flynn told police that he kept a gun in the console, but no weapon was found there.
Prosecutors alleged that Flynn, 40, staged the home invasion to mislead investigators and shared thoughts of killing his wife, 37, in text messages to his then-mistress. Authorities never found the gun used in the killing.
“The evidence has proven the defendant’s account to be a complete fabrication,” Matthew C. Joseph, assistant prosecuting attorney for the Miami County Prosecuting Attorney’s Office in Troy, Ohio, said in closings Tuesday.
Flynn, who had tears on his face, wiped his nose.
“While the defendant told law enforcement that he was sleeping, his electronic devices documented something different. They documented movement and activity in the hours leading up to Ashley’s murder,” Joseph said. “The defendant said he was sleeping. His devices say he was awake and moving.”
Joseph told the court that Flynn “wanted to be a victim” and wanted to “keep his mistress and have his daughters all to himself.”
“Being the victim allowed him to do that without being the husband who left his wife for a mistress,” Joseph said. “Instead, he’d be the husband whose wife was tragically murdered by an unknown intruder.”
Over eight days, the jury heard from 40 prosecution witnesses, including Alleigha Botner, who said she met Flynn when she was 20 and an intern at his church. She said they had been having an affair at the time of Ashley’s killing.
Botner, now 24, testified that Flynn had made remarks that he hated his wife and harbored thoughts of killing her. Botner sobbed on the stand as she read some of their text messages, telling the court that she regretted telling him in one message: “I want to kill her, Caleb.”
Botner said Flynn replied: “That makes two of us.”
In other text messages shown in court, Flynn discussed wanting his wife dead.
“I was up until 4 a.m. last night crying, literally trying to think of ways to kill her and not go to jail,” he allegedly wrote in an August 2025 text, about six months before the killing.
In another text, Botner said she wasn’t serious. “I’m not asking that you take her life obviously, because that’s not what you should do, and I know you actually wouldn’t,” she wrote. “But to make the divorce happen, it would change everything.”
Botner told the court that her feelings about Flynn have since changed and she hated him. When a prosecutor asked her why, she said: “Because I believe that he murdered his wife.”
The defense rested Monday without calling a single witness.
Flynn’s attorney, Patrick Mulligan, said in his closing argument that being “unfaithful doesn’t equal murder.”
“This case is wholly lacking in concrete evidence. Connecting a couple of meaningless dots doesn’t solve the case,” he said.
Flynn sang in the televised auditions in Chicago for Season 12 of “American Idol” in 2013 but did not advance to the main competition. He faces life in prison without the possibility of parole.

articles.title_zh: Jack Smith, Former Special Counsel Who Charged Trump, Appears Before Congress: Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
Special counsel Jack Smith, who brought two indictments against now-President Donald Trump in 2023, testified in front of Congress again on Tuesday — this time, to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
Smith’s testimony comes as Republicans continue to probe the investigations into Trump and as some in the party, including the president, have pushed for often-unspecified criminal charges to be brought against Smith.
Here are the major takeaways from Tuesday’s hearing.
Republicans have struggled mightily to substantiate Trump’s desire for Smith to be charged criminally . But rarely has it seemed to backfire like it did Tuesday .
Sen. Eric Schmitt of Missouri crafted an apparent conspiracy theory about Smith being tied to the prosecution of Trump in Fulton County, Georgia. To substantiate his theory, Schmitt cited text messages he suggested showed Smith had been at an Atlanta Hawks game on February 3, 2024 – the day after Fulton County prosecutor Fani Willis and special prosecutor Nathan Wade admitted to an affair.
Smith appeared dumbfounded, though. He denied going to a Hawks game and said he had no recollection of even being in Atlanta.
“What would you say if I had a series of text messages from your team that said you were in Atlanta at a Warriors-Hawks game on February 3, 2024 – the day after Willis and Wade announced their affair?” Schmitt said.
Schmitt went big on the allegation, telling Smith, “I don’t think you know that we have this stuff.” He urged Smith not to “perjure yourself.” He later called Smith a “dirtbag.” He later told the “Charlie Kirk Show” that he was just asking questions and seeing whether Smith would ensnare himself.
Eventually, Democrats got Schmitt to allow Smith to actually review the evidence – a poster featuring the texts in question. In one of them, a fellow prosecutor asks about a seat being reserved for Smith. The poster showed the Atlanta Hawks’ arena.
But by this point, Smith seemed to put it together. He said he was not at a game featuring the Atlanta Hawks , but rather the University of Iowa Hawkeyes women’s basketball team – which then featured Caitlin Clark – at the University of Maryland in the Washington, DC, area.
Smith’s recollection matches up with a game played that day.
Sen. Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota, after clearing up the matter, said Schmitt should apologize.
Schmitt’s office has not responded a request for comment.
At the hearing, he maintained that the texts “could have obviously been related to the prosecution” in Fulton County. He said he stood by calling Smith a “dirtbag.”
The scene epitomized how speculative and thinly constructed the GOP’s allegations about Smith, Trump’s foes and about the justice system being weaponized against Trump have been. Likewise, the GOP’s other major perjury allegation against Smith rests on a complete misreading of the evidence .
But rarely has this apparent fishing expedition been laid so bare. Schmitt seemed to firmly believe he had nailed Smith on something. But just minutes later, it seemed to fall apart – and rather spectacularly so.
Smith is a very careful witness. He often pauses noticeably before answering a question — in a way that can be a little jarring.
But he’s also made clear that he wants to fight back against the Trump administration’s weaponization of the justice system against people like him. And on Tuesday, he was a little more animated and open.
He punctuated his opening statement by saying, “Fear may be contagious; courage is as well.”
He also called it an “outrage” that people he worked with were “targeted illegally, lost their jobs illegally, and had their lives turned upside down by this Department of Justice.”
When asked about the Supreme Court’s 2024 ruling conferring presidents with a large degree of immunity, Smith said it “can be very dangerous for the rule of law” for powerful people to benefit from such exceptions.
He also jousted with lawmakers a little more than he did before, rather than dryly reciting facts.
When GOP Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas asked him whether he had any regrets, Smith said he regretted that “the people I worked with have been unfairly fired and vilified.”
When  Republican Sen. Darline Graham of South Carolina claimed Smith unfairly targeted the phone records of her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, Smith told her that Lindsey Graham had investigated Trump’s underlying voter-fraud claims and found them to be false.
And he said he won’t be going away quietly.
“I will not be silenced by the continued threats of prosecution from the president or others,” Smith said.
That exchange with Darline Graham was also significant when it comes to learning something new about the attempted prosecutions of Trump.
The reason: Smith said Lindsey Graham was likely to be a witness in the case.
“I believe your brother was a patriotic public servant,” Smith said. “He was not a target of our investigation. In fact, he likely would have been a witness in our case. Your brother investigated the claims that Donald Trump was making. He found them to be false.”
Lindsey Graham publicly broke with Trump on the Senate floor after January 6 (i.e. “ count me out ”) and appeared to be initially helpful to investigators probing the situation.
He later reconciled with Trump and assailed Smith’s investigation when he was among those whose phone records were wrapped up in the probe — and even pushed to get a financial payout for it.
Smith’s comments suggest Graham could have played at least some role in proving the charges against Trump.
The former special counsel seemed to make a point to repeatedly vouch for members of his former staff  who were fired by Trump’s Justice Department and, in some cases, were repeatedly invoked by name at Tuesday’s hearing.
Smith even called them “heroes.”
“My view: These people are heroes, and I believe our country does not recognize and pay enough attention to people like that,” he said. “I think if we did, the partisan things that we’re discussing today – a lot of that would go away.”
Smith also warned about what ousting people like that would portend for the country.
“If you drive those people out of public service, the institutions we rely on for justice, for protecting our country — those institutions are weakened,” Smith said.
When Democratic Sen. Adam Schiff of California talked about how Smith had been attacked, Smith said it was “much more important that the public servants who I work with – that we stop vilifying public servants.”
It’s been nearly a year since Trump appeared alongside then-Attorney General Pam Bondi and claimed Smith had committed crimes.
“Hopefully the Attorney General is looking at what he’s done,” Trump added eight months ago on social media.
There’s been little since then to suggest the Trump administration is able to provide him what he wants. And Tuesday’s hearing often felt like going through the motions more so than anything else.
Apart from Schmitt’s attempt at a gotcha, other Republican lawmakers generally mined territory already covered in the January House Judiciary Committee hearing .
Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri and others repeated an allegation from months ago that Smith perjured himself with his denials about seeking the contents of lawmakers’ communications. But Smith pointed to the holes in that previously debunked theory.
Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana at one point tried to suggest that Smith might have lobbied to become special counsel — the implication being that he had a political agenda and was targeting Trump — but when Smith denied it, Kennedy moved on.
Smith also told lawmakers that he sought to keep secret the phone and other records he was seeking because of concerns that Trump and his allies would try to obstruct justice .
When lawmakers suggested that Smith was implying with the nondisclosure requests that they couldn’t be trusted not to destroy evidence, Smith said it was actually Trump he was worried about.
